metadata.note: The Lehigh Valley's Seneca Falls Branch, 18.4 miles from Geneva Junction on the main line east to Cayuga Junction, with a 1.6-mile spur into Seneca Falls village. It began as the Seneca County Railroad, opened in 1897 from the Lehigh Valley main line just south of the branch's bridge over the Seneca River, south-east of Geneva, and its whole reason for existing is visible on the map: it was built along the SOUTH bank of the Seneca River to compete with the New York Central's Auburn Road, which already ran along the north bank through Waterloo and Seneca Falls. The two lines shadow each other for miles. Passenger service ran from the opening but was never well used and ended in September 1914. East of L.V. Junction the Lehigh Valley owned no track at all: the last six miles to Cayuga Junction, where it met the Auburn and Ithaca branch, were run over New York Central rails. The line went in pieces -- the Seneca Falls spur in 1959, Geneva Junction to L.V. Junction in 1969, and the Cayuga end in 1971. Most of the western half is now the Cayuga-Seneca Canal Trail. See lehigh_valley_railroad.geojson for the main line this left at Geneva Junction and lehigh_valley_finger_lakes_branches.geojson for the Auburn and Ithaca branch it reached at Cayuga Junction.
sources: https://nyrails.org/railroads/lehigh-valley-railroad/lehigh-valley-railroad-seneca-falls-branch/ (New York Railroad Archive): the branch ran 18.4 miles from Geneva Junction, where it connected to the Lehigh Valley main line, to Cayuga Junction, where it connected to the Auburn and Ithaca branch, with a 1.6-mile spur from Seneca Junction into Seneca Falls village. Stations and mileposts: Geneva Junction 0.0, Waterloo 4.8, Seneca Junction 6.8, L.V. Junction 12.5, Cayuga 14.6, Cayuga Junction 18.4. Between L.V. Junction and Cayuga Junction, six miles, the railroad ran over the tracks of the New York Central Railroad. Abandonments: the Seneca Junction to Seneca Falls spur in 1959, Geneva Junction to L.V. Junction in 1969, and Cayuga to Cayuga Junction in 1971. The page states outright that its author is not sure when the line was built or by whom.

https://www.fltimes.com/lifestyle/way-back-when-in-seneca-county-rail-service-south-of-seneca-river/article_23db766a-d35f-11e6-9b31-731ae2944830.html and https://railroad.net/notes-on-lehigh-valley-seneca-falls-branch-t153339.html: in 1897 the Seneca County Railroad opened from the Lehigh Valley main line just south of that branch's bridge over the Seneca River, south-east of Geneva, built on the south side of the Seneca River at least partially to compete with the 'Auburn Road' branch of the New York Central on the river's north side. The eastern terminus was at Ovid Street in Seneca Falls, where a combination passenger and freight facility was built; in Waterloo an existing building at the Fayette Street crossing was used as a passenger station. The main line was 8.2 miles long, single track, standard gauge, 76-pound rail except for one mile of 80-pound steel. Passenger service commenced when the branch opened, patronage was never good, and service was discontinued by the end of September 1914. In 1958 the stub-end of the line from Seneca Junction (Kingdom Road) along the canal into Seneca Falls was abandoned.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: When and how the Lehigh Valley took the Seneca County Railroad over -- nyrails says plainly it does not know who built the line or when, and no acquisition date was found, so the company is given here as 'Seneca County Railroad / Lehigh Valley Railroad' without a transition year. The two sources also disagree by a year on the Seneca Falls spur, 1958 against 1959; 1959 is used and the conflict is noted. All frequencies are estimates -- passenger service was sparse and freight-only years are given a nominal daily headway. The 8.2-mile figure in the second source appears to describe the Seneca County Railroad's own line (Geneva Junction to Seneca Junction plus the spur is 8.4 miles) rather than the full 18.4-mile Lehigh Valley branch, but that reading is inference, not sourced. Separately: the Finger Lakes Times says the line was extended east to Cayuga in 1904, connecting with the New York Central at Lehigh Valley Junction, but the branch is drawn over its full Geneva Junction-Cayuga Junction length from 1897. If the 1904 date is right, the eastern 10 miles (L.V. Junction to Cayuga Junction) are drawn seven years early and the feature should be split at L.V. Junction into a 1897-1914 western half and a 1904-1914 eastern half. nyrails does not mention an extension either way, so this is unresolved rather than settled.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API, taken by NAME rather than by generic shortest-path routing: OSM carries 32 ways explicitly named 'Seneca Falls Branch' (railway=abandoned/dismantled) for the middle of the line, the western right-of-way survives as the 'Cayuga-Seneca Canal Trail' tagged railway=abandoned, and the six miles of trackage rights follow the ex-NYC line OSM names 'Auburn Secondary' (railway=rail), truncated at the booked 5.9 miles. This matters here because the surviving active track on this corridor is the New York Central's line on the NORTH bank; routing generically would have drawn the wrong railroad.

Every section was checked against the nyrails mileposts: Geneva Junction-Waterloo 7.29 km against 7.72 booked (0.94x); Waterloo-L.V. Junction 12.61 km against 12.39 (1.02x); L.V. Junction-Cayuga Junction 9.61 km against 9.50 (1.01x); and the Seneca Falls spur 2.54 km against 2.57 (0.99x), diverging from the main line at MP 6.8, which is Seneca Junction. The assembled main line comes to 29.46 km against the booked 18.4 miles (29.61 km), a 0.5% match. No straight-line approximations were needed anywhere on this layer.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.freight_only_audit: 2026-08-26, Rule 1. This layer drew the branch through 1971 and the Seneca Falls spur through 1959 on abandonment dates, not service dates. Removed three freight-only segments: the branch's 1914-1969 segment (its own note began 'Freight only.'), the branch's 1969-1971 segment (the Cayuga to Cayuga Junction stub, six miles of which the Lehigh Valley did not even own, running on New York Central rails), and the spur's 1914-1959 segment. Passenger service on this branch ended at the end of September 1914 -- confirmed by the Finger Lakes Times and by the September 1914 discontinuance hearing, which recorded about one passenger a day -- and the Lehigh Valley ended all passenger service system-wide on Feb. 4 1961, so nothing on this layer may be drawn past 1914. The abandonment dates (spur 1959, Geneva Junction-L.V. Junction 1969, Cayuga-Cayuga Junction 1971, rails lifted by 1975) are kept as context in the surviving segment notes. Both features now draw 1897-1914 only.

segments.note: The Seneca County Railroad opened Oct. 24 1897 from the Lehigh Valley main line just south of the branch's bridge over the Seneca River, south-east of Geneva. It was deliberately built along the SOUTH side of the Seneca River, at least partly to compete with the New York Central's 'Auburn Road' on the north bank. Single track, standard gauge, 76-pound rail except for a mile of 80-pound steel. The Seneca County Railway merged into the Lehigh Valley on Aug. 3 1903 and the line became the Seneca Falls Branch. East of L.V. Junction (MP 12.5) the Lehigh Valley owned no track at all -- the last six miles to Cayuga Junction, where it met the Auburn and Ithaca branch, ran over the New York Central. Passenger service ran from the opening but was never used: at the September 1914 hearing on the railroad's application to drop it, the branch was shown to be carrying about one passenger a day, with average daily passenger revenue of 16.6 cents in July and 41.7 cents in August against a cost of $5.07 a day. It ended by the end of September 1914. Freight continued for decades afterwards -- Geneva Junction to L.V. Junction was abandoned in 1969 and the Cayuga to Cayuga Junction end in 1971, with the rails lifted by 1975 -- but no passengers rode after 1914, and the Lehigh Valley ran its last passenger train anywhere on Feb. 4 1961. Most of the western half is now the Cayuga-Seneca Canal Trail; frequency estimated, unsourced
sources: Segment-level: the 1897 opening and the September 1914 end of passenger service were both checked against the sources below. The Finger Lakes Times gives the opening as Oct. 24 1897, the merger into the Lehigh Valley as Aug. 3 1903, and passenger service as discontinued in late 1914; the September 1914 discontinuance hearing recorded about one passenger a day. The headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: A 1.6-mile spur running from Seneca Junction, at Kingdom Road, along the canal into Seneca Falls village, where a combination passenger and freight station stood at Ovid Street. In Waterloo, back on the main branch, an existing building at the Fayette Street crossing served as the passenger station. Passenger service ended with the rest of the branch at the end of September 1914; freight continued until the stub was abandoned in 1959 (one account gives 1958); frequency estimated, unsourced
